RT Alex Imas
I joined @GoogleDeepMind to develop a research program on the economics of AGI. Today, together with Andrew Koh (@andrewjkoh) and Shane Legg (@ShaneLegg), we are incredibly excited to release The Economics of Intelligence, the first in a series of projects from our group on how AGI will change the economy.

How do capability improvements transform the economy, and when? In this project, we define thresholds of economic capabilities, e.g., minimal AGI, based on how they transform the economy. We then track how the economy–market structure, employment, and wages–changes during the transition across capability regimes.

We have seen exponential increases in what AI agents can do but the broader economy seems almost remarkably unchanged. Part of the reason is that the solo AI agent is the wrong economic object; economic transformation is an equilibrium outcome where organizations compete. Looking at how intelligence functions within organizations, transformation will depend on when two key capability thresholds are crossed: competence (gains on individual skills, e.g., coding, math) and coordination (gains on ability of agents to cooperate and work together).

We show that what economic transformation looks like depends on whether AI becomes supercompetent, supercooperative, or both—the regime of artificial superintelligence (ASI). Tracking this transition shows why the real visible transformation may come from improvements in coordination—a capability most benchmarks don’t yet track. Past a certain threshold, AI capabilities can break the Coasian ceiling on firm size and lead to an economy that looks drastically different than the one we see today.

Two main takeaways:
1. To understand the path of transformation, we should be tracking agentic coordination more closely.
2. The impact of AI will likely show up in wages before market structure or employment.

We are really excited about this paper. Excited to hear people’s thoughts.

Link: https://institute.deepmind.com/essays/the-economics-of-intelligence/

This research gets at something missing from most debates about AI’s economic impact: coordination.

Organizations are more than the sum of their best performers, so smarter individual agents won’t transform the economy on their own. Agents that can coordinate together might do.

Lower cost per task doesn’t always come from lower token prices.

On Agent Arena, GPT-6.1 Sol (Max) by @OpenAI costs $1.91 per task:

API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions

Earlier this month Anthropic announced a generous new benefit for their Max and Team subscriptions: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers would get the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits to use with the Anthropic API.

 OpenAI have now launched pretty much exactly the same deal: if you have a $100, $200, or $500 subscription plan with them you now get that same quantity of credits to apply to one of your API organizations.

 I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me! I may even ship some public-facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions.

blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
blogs.description: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how…
blogs.content:
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.

 Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.

 I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

 By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

 Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.

 Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.

 This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

 A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]

 We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

 My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.

 Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:

 Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.

 These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

 Tags: game-design , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , agentic-engineering , claude-mythos-fable

blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,742 new readers. Google spent much of 2026 playing catch-up in the AI race. A month and two frontier models later, it’s sitting at the top of the charts again, sort of.
 Gemini 4 Carbon has the numbers to back up all the comeback talk, but like Argon at launch, the public can’t use it yet — and with OpenAI and Anthropic shipping at a similar pace, the crown might not last long.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Google’s Carbon takes the benchmark crown (for now)

 Nate’s Notebook: Hire a dispatcher first

 Turn a prompt into a poster with Canva Craft

 An Anthropic manager bets on junior engineers

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 GOOGLE
 💎  Google’s Carbon takes the benchmark crown (for now)
 Image source: Google

 The Rundown: Google just unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon, a new frontier model built for cybersecurity and long-running coding work that tops 15 of 17 benchmarks on Google’s charts, but isn’t yet public — with only select cyber defenders gaining access to start.
 The details:
 Carbon’s 59 on Artificial Analysis’ “Intelligence Index” takes the top spot from Claude Opus 5.5 and improves 9 points over Google’s Argon from four weeks ago.

 Carbon’s widest wins over OpenAI’s Astra and Opus came on long-input reasoning (+24 points), hacking (+12), workflow automation (+11), and math (+8).

 Carbon’s $2/$10 intro API price (per million tokens in/out) is half of Opus 5.5’s and 1/5 of Astra’s, though it doubles to Opus’s rate after the initial discount.

 Google hasn’t given a date for wider access to Carbon, with Argon previously rolling out around two weeks after its debut to cyber defenders.

 Why it matters: Two big models in weeks is a big statement from a Google that spent much of 2026 playing catch-up, and Carbon’s numbers back it up. But nobody outside select cyber defenders can vibe-check those numbers yet, and at the pace OpenAI and Anthropic are shipping, the rankings could change well before Carbon goes public.

 TOGETHER WITH GARTNER
 📖  AI activity isn't the same as value    

 The Rundown: 86% of CIOs say AI risk is growing faster than value — four times faster, on average. These Gartner IT Symposium/Xpo takeaways show CIOs how to compound value, not just activity, and govern AI before risk erodes advantage.
 Learn how to:
 Balance AI value and risk

 Govern AI through an AI central bank

 Fill AI safety gaps with human oversight

 Download the insights .

 NATE’S NOTEBOOK
 ☕ Nate’s Notebook: Hire a dispatcher first

 The Rundown:   Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.
 Nate: Most mornings, I brain dump my project list into my phone while I wait for coffee. Dot splits that one voice dump into separate chats running at once, each in its own context window. By the time I’m back at my desk, they’re gathering context, doing research, and drafting outlines.
 That’s the difference between the agents landing right now. Grok Bot and OpenClaw are monothreads: one worker running unattended. Even with careful rules and profiles, I’ve never been super impressed with that work. Dot is a delegator, handing discrete jobs to threads I can still coach.
 Unattended is the hard part. Think about hiring a new assistant: we all underestimate how hard it is for anyone, human or agent, to anticipate what matters to you. Agents will get there, but it takes time and a lot more context. Until then, I stay in the loop for chunking, quality, and coaching.
 Last week, I laid out my ladder: read, then write, then send. If you’re not ready for write access, that’s okay. Dot sorts the noise in my inbox and flags what needs me, with no access to write anything. Just letting it read and triage is a smart, useful, powerful first step, and it’s why I’m even more excited to finally get Anthropic’s Duet.
 No Dot yet? The brain dump works in a new ChatGPT voice chat, too.
 We’re currently in the messy middle. Triage and delegation are worth jumping into now; figure out the rest along the way.

 AI TRAINING
 🎨  Turn a prompt into a poster with Canva Craft

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try Canva’s new image model on a workshop poster. You’ll check the headline, add event details you can edit, and make a square version without rebuilding the whole artwork.
 Step-by-step:
 Open Dream Lab from Canva’s homepage and select Craft. Choose a portrait layout and check your AI allowance before generating

 Paste the guide’s brief. Ask for a clear headline and blank space for the event details. Then, check the headline very closely

 If the issue remains after one revision, generate the artwork without text and add the heading yourself

 Open the image in Canva and add the date, time, and venue as text boxes. Try Magic Layers only if you need to edit words or objects inside the generated image

 Make a square version and change the event date in both designs. Check the downloaded files for spelling, cropping, and the correct details

 Pro tip: Keep details that may change in ordinary text boxes. A new date should not require another image generation. You can find our full guide, test resources, and prompts here .

 PRESENTED BY ENEY BY MACPAW
 💬  Just ask. Skip to done.

 The Rundown: Eney by MacPaw is a proactive AI assistant that takes tedious work and life tasks off your list on Mac and iPhone. It spots what needs attention and handles tasks with your go-ahead.
 With Eney, you can:
 Act on what’s on your screen with Eney Wand

 Delegate tasks, big and small

 Work seamlessly across your favorite apps

 Get started with Eney .

 AI & THE WORKFORCE
 🤝  An Anthropic manager bets on junior engineers
 Image source: Felix Rieseberg / J. M. W. Turner

 The Rundown: Anthropic engineering manager Felix Rieseberg wrote that he’s dropped the coding interview from his team’s hiring, saying Claude now outperforms people on the short coding tests it relied on — while also offering an optimistic counter-take that AI is letting junior engineers overtake veterans.
 The details:
 Rieseberg, who has led engineering on Claude Code Desktop, says he has seen newer engineers “fly past” likely better coders, and that “hunger beats tenure.”

 His advice to juniors is to tie one bold idea to higher-ups’ goals and build it as a weekend prototype, since with AI “execution isn’t expensive anymore.”

 He used Claude Code’s desktop app as an example, with two newer employees prototyping it in one weekend before it went public just over a week later.

 Why it matters: A lot of this year’s talk about junior engineers has been gloomy, with Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark saying earlier that AI makes their value “a bit more dubious.” Rieseberg’s taking the opposite stance from inside the same company, with a vote of confidence in agency and AI-enabled ambition over years of experience.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Mario built an AI prospector that pitches websites to local shops
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Mario Mitchell:
 “ I built a set of agents that run every day to find local businesses with no website, build a site for a selected business, and email the mockup to that lead. It’s for anyone who sells web services to local businesses and wants to automate the prospecting.
 Each day, my Gemini and ChatGPT agents check the major cities in the state I select, for the industry I select, and find the best businesses that don’t have a website. They add those businesses to a spreadsheet. A second agent reads the spreadsheet, selects the best prospect based on its need for web services and likelihood of buying, and starts building its website.
 That agent checks the business’s social media for images and its Google Business Profile for information. It also looks for a logo. If there isn’t one, it creates a logo for them. A third agent takes the mockup and sends an email with it to the lead. A fourth agent is set up to reply once the lead responds, book them on a call, and put the call on the calendar.”
 See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

 Artificial Analysis   released v5 of its “Intelligence Index” AI leaderboard, now relying more on private tests, with Chinese open models falling further behind in the rankings and OpenAI’s new Terra model outperforming despite its mid-tier level.
 New AI startup Particle   released Particle-1, a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash variant trained to reason less on coding tasks, using ~45% fewer tokens with near-identical accuracy.

blogs.name: Stratechery by Ben Thompson
blogs.title: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description:
Listen to this post: Good morning,

Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar. Sankar has worked at…
blogs.content:
Listen to this post:

 Good morning,

 Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar . Sankar has worked at Palantir for 20 years, and has taken on an increasingly visible role as public intellectual, including authoring the book Mobilize , an exhortation “To Reboot the American Industrial Base and Stop World War III”. I previously interviewed Sankar in June 2023 . That interview is a great place to start in terms of understanding Palantir, which we mostly discuss in this interview in the context of AI.

 To that end, in this interview we discuss why Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion, why companies focused on the top-line have more success adopting AI, and why he is frustrated at the labs refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety. Then we discuss what Palantir has learned from AI, how companies can preserve alpha instead of the median, and whether or not we need more models. Sankar also explains exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is, why tech is in a religious war, and his retrospective on Anthropic’s battle with the U.S. government.

 This Interview is presented by Stripe, the economic infrastructure of AI, and for Stratechery itself.

 As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

 On to the Interview:

 An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War

 This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

 Topics:

 Diffusing Intelligence | Top Line vs. Bottom Line | Safety and Systems Engineering | Palantir’s AI Lessons | Alpha vs. Beta | Model Questions | Forward-Deployed Engineering | Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government | AI Religion

 Background

 Shyam Sankar, welcome back to Stratechery.

 SS: Ben, thanks for having me back.

 Well, the last time we talked was in conjunction with Ted Mabrey , the head of Palantir Commercial. As is usually the case with dual interviews, we got right down to business — and I do have to say, I do a lot of interviews where I usually kind of know where I want to go, but that one was super helpful to me in understanding Palantir and thinking about AI generally . But before we get into that, we never got to do my traditional background questions — where you came from, how you got to where you are. So for you, do we start in Orlando, in Lagos, or in India?

 SS: At least Lagos. My father, in his early 20s, moved to Lagos and built one of the first pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in all of Africa. He set up this whole life there for the better part of ten years. I was born in India, but really I grew up until I was three in Lagos.

 And then there was this horrible armed robbery that happened at the house — they decapitated the dog, pistol-whipped my father, and threatened my mother. So we left all of our earthly possessions behind and started over again in Orlando, which ended up being a truly phenomenal place to grow up. The profound optimism of Disney World, the shadow of the Space Coast , seeing shuttle launches in elementary school, running into your courtyard filled with this sense of optimism about how technology will inevitably lead to a better world — which, if you fast-forward twenty years from the ’80s, I think kids were fed a very different diet of Terminator and “ nature always finds a way “, “How dare man try to do anything that creates progress?”, so that’s really where it started.

 Is that actually the ultimate example of man overcoming nature — not the space shuttle, but in fact Disney World?

 SS: (laughing) That’s true! The fact that millions of people go there every year, to the middle of the swamp — and it’s fantastic, a lot of fun.

 What does meritocracy mean to you? I was reading the recent profile of you in Colossus , and it opened with [Palantir CEO] Alex Karp’s statements in that regard, but it was put in the context of you growing up in Orlando, taking an entrance exam to go to Trinity High School, and how that launched you into what you became. Is that a sentiment from Alex, is it from you, or what’s your take?

 SS: It’s a sentiment for both of us, for different reasons. We’re both kind of acquired tastes, in many ways, and living in a world that judges you by the fruits you bear, rather than any dimension you have no control over, is obviously a better world to live in. I think it’s a precondition to the American Dream.

 I was going to ask you that. Because you have this background — born in India, originally living in Lagos, come to America. What does being an American mean to you? Is that the same question, or is there some tension between those two things?

 SS: They overlap profoundly. Being an American is this profound belief in your own human agency, and the community you’re in, and the ability to create a more perfect union — the recognition, the ability to hold the contradiction, that not everything is perfect today but it’s incumbent on us to make it better. That may sound a little Pollyannish and even corny, but that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Everywhere else, people are profoundly cynical — things are the way they are — and there’s a very thin line between cynicism and nihilism, and you kind of give up on everything. That’s the death spiral, that’s how you get the Dark Ages.

 After university and graduate school, you worked on Xoom, on remittances — and then you go to work for Palantir.

 SS: Xoom with an X.

 Xoom with an X, that’s right. Not the Zoom with a Z — which maybe I shouldn’t be talking to, since you’re now an executive at Palantir using Zoom with a Z, but that’s another discussion. You worked on Xoom and remittances, then Palantir, working on national security, arguing for building our homegrown industrial base. There’s an argument there that — to take a paradox that’s maybe unfair — how do you go from a career focused on sending money out of America to being an advocate for money here in America, rebuilding our capital base? Is there tension there, or am I creating paradoxes out of thin air to build a theme?

 SS: I think you’re creating a bit of a paradox out of thin air. First of all, there’s a policy question — if you have a working class trying to get money to support their family, how can they do that as efficiently as possible?

 The bigger issue is the profound lie of globalization. The calculus that globalization got wrong is this idea that we can do the innovation and “they” can do the production — “they” make the things, we do the innovation. The problem is that innovation is a consequence of productivity, if you stop making the thing, you cede the stimulus required to do the innovation around the thing.

 The example I always give young computer scientists is, what do you think motivated Google to do the research behind “ Attention Is All You Need “? If you talk to that team, they wanted the 3% improvement in Google Translate. You cannot think of something more prosaic leading to something more profound. So we should be very careful where we give up — we buy a little too much into comparative advantage and give up the stimulus for production.

 Why do you think — what leads to that mistake of thinking that it’s okay to just own the inputs and not worry about the outputs?

 SS: Because at the margin, it’s true. At the margin, you can hire WuXi as a cheap set of hands at the lab bench to do a little bit of work. But at the limit, that’s a transfer of knowledge. At every increment it seems to make sense — you’re still doing the innovation — until one day you wake up and realize, “Oh, I don’t have it anymore”.

 Diffusing Intelligence

 You’re the only Stratechery interview that I’ve offered a job to. You sent over a list of questions you wanted me to talk about, and I have to say they’re really good — I did ask if you wanted to prepare all my interviews going forward, I don’t think I got a response, maybe the email got lost.

 SS: (laughing) I’m thinking about it.

 Okay, good. Well, let’s drill in — we’ll take your outline, why not, go through it and talk about it, and I think there are themes that might emerge. So number one, and this is from Shyam Sankar, does this count as a Shyam bomb, by the way, the long extended email detailing what we should talk about?

 SS: It’s not nearly vitriolic enough, so you’re spared.

 Got it, that makes sense. Number one, is the AI industry solving the wrong bottleneck? You argue we are over-investing intellectually in the supply of intelligence and under-investing in diffusion. Tell me what you mean.

 SS: If you thought about a crass metaphor of AI through electricity — there are people who generate the electrons, the power producers — for electricity to have any impact on our economy, there needed to be other people who built machine tools that run on those electrons. And that led to a profound revolution. Not only would you introduce one piece of machinery into your factory, you’d start redesigning your factories around the fact that we have electrons.

 Let’s call that diffusion, how does the miracle of electricity diffuse into the economy? There’s a similar question with AI. I think we are very focused on how to make better models, smarter models, more machine intelligence — and we should keep doing that — but we’re very under-indexed on how to accelerate the rate of diffusion. Where is the economic value being created? How do we turn these tokens into economic value more quickly with a great ratio around it? I’m obsessed with that, because I think there’s a license to operate in society where the benefits of this stuff diffusing really do matter and I think we’re getting the calculus around some of this pretty wrong.

 So who is “we”? Who are the ones insufficiently focused on diffusion? Who are you trying to convince here?

 SS: I think the labs are, but in general the entire market structure. People are being rewarded — and it’s very rational, if you’re a lab, you’ve been in your own reinforcement-learning loop, you do fundamental research, you make a more powerful model, and your valuation doubles or quadruples and every year it seems to keep working. Baked into that is the idea that eventually this stuff will diffuse, eventually there will be economic value.

 But one of the conceits I’m not sure people are getting right is, what is the atomic unit of the enterprise? Let’s leave consumer out of this. The presumption, as expressed through the product strategy you see from the labs, is that the atomic unit of the enterprise is the knowledge worker — if I can make every worker more productive, that’s the ROI, and that’s not actually true. The atomic unit of the enterprise is the workflow, you can make a single supply-chain analyst more productive and generate no incremental ROI, you have to make the entire supply-chain workflow measurably more productive to capture the value.

 There are some roles where the cardinality collapses — the knowledge worker is the workflow, like coding — so you have perfect product-market fit for those things, and you can chase unbounded productivity. But that’s a very small part of everything we do in the real economy.

 Again, I don’t understand the audience here. In a market, shouldn’t the model makers just do their job, which is making better models, and then there are lots of opportunities for companies to take those models and diffuse them? Isn’t that what Palantir is trying to do? Who is the target of this exhortation?

 SS: To those wondering, “Okay, we’re creating this, we’re spending trillions of dollars, where’s the return, how’s it working, why is the best example of excellence an AI assistant, which is nice and convenient but that’s not going to inflect our GDP?”. An interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar about AI diffusion and safety, forward-deployed engineer, and what the battle in tech is actually about.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar . Sankar has worked at Palantir for 20 years, and has taken on an increasingly visible role as public intellectual, including authoring the book Mobilize , an exhortation “To Reboot the American Industrial Base and Stop World War III”. I previously interviewed Sankar in June 2023 . That interview is a great place to start in terms of understanding Palantir, which we mostly discuss in this interview in the context of AI.

To that end, in this interview we discuss why Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion, why companies focused on the top-line have more success adopting AI, and why he is frustrated at the labs refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety. Then we discuss what Palantir has learned from AI, how companies can preserve alpha instead of the median, and whether or not we need more models. Sankar also explains exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is, why tech is in a religious war, and his retrospective on Anthropic’s battle with the U.S. government.

This Interview is presented by Stripe, the economic infrastructure of AI, and for Stratechery itself.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

Topics:

Diffusing Intelligence | Top Line vs. Bottom Line | Safety and Systems Engineering | Palantir’s AI Lessons | Alpha vs. Beta | Model Questions | Forward-Deployed Engineering | Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government | AI Religion

Background

Shyam Sankar, welcome back to Stratechery.

SS: Ben, thanks for having me back.

Well, the last time we talked was in conjunction with Ted Mabrey , the head of Palantir Commercial. As is usually the case with dual interviews, we got right down to business — and I do have to say, I do a lot of interviews where I usually kind of know where I want to go, but that one was super helpful to me in understanding Palantir and thinking about AI generally . But before we get into that, we never got to do my traditional background questions — where you came from, how you got to where you are. So for you, do we start in Orlando, in Lagos, or in India?

SS: At least Lagos. My father, in his early 20s, moved to Lagos and built one of the first pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in all of Africa. He set up this whole life there for the better part of ten years. I was born in India, but really I grew up until I was three in Lagos.

And then there was this horrible armed robbery that happened at the house — they decapitated the dog, pistol-whipped my father, and threatened my mother. So we left all of our earthly possessions behind and started over again in Orlando, which ended up being a truly phenomenal place to grow up. The profound optimism of Disney World, the shadow of the Space Coast , seeing shuttle launches in elementary school, running into your courtyard filled with this sense of optimism about how technology will inevitably lead to a better world — which, if you fast-forward twenty years from the ’80s, I think kids were fed a very different diet of Terminator and “ nature always finds a way “, “How dare man try to do anything that creates progress?”, so that’s really where it started.

Is that actually the ultimate example of man overcoming nature — not the space shuttle, but in fact Disney World?

SS: (laughing) That’s true! The fact that millions of people go there every year, to the middle of the swamp — and it’s fantastic, a lot of fun.

What does meritocracy mean to you? I was reading the recent profile of you in Colossus , and it opened with [Palantir CEO] Alex Karp’s statements in that regard, but it was put in the context of you growing up in Orlando, taking an entrance exam to go to Trinity High School, and how that launched you into what you became. Is that a sentiment from Alex, is it from you, or what’s your take?

SS: It’s a sentiment for both of us, for different reasons. We’re both kind of acquired tastes, in many ways, and living in a world that judges you by the fruits you bear, rather than any dimension you have no control over, is obviously a better world to live in. I think it’s a precondition to the American Dream.

I was going to ask you that. Because you have this background — born in India, originally living in Lagos, come to America. What does being an American mean to you? Is that the same question, or is there some tension between those two things?

SS: They overlap profoundly. Being an American is this profound belief in your own human agency, and the community you’re in, and the ability to create a more perfect union — the recognition, the ability to hold the contradiction, that not everything is perfect today but it’s incumbent on us to make it better. That may sound a little Pollyannish and even corny, but that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Everywhere else, people are profoundly cynical — things are the way they are — and there’s a very thin line between cynicism and nihilism, and you kind of give up on everything. That’s the death spiral, that’s how you get the Dark Ages.

After university and graduate school, you worked on Xoom, on remittances — and then you go to work for Palantir.

SS: Xoom with an X.

Xoom with an X, that’s right. Not the Zoom with a Z — which maybe I shouldn’t be talking to, since you’re now an executive at Palantir using Zoom with a Z, but that’s another discussion. You worked on Xoom and remittances, then Palantir, working on national security, arguing for building our homegrown industrial base. There’s an argument there that — to take a paradox that’s maybe unfair — how do you go from a career focused on sending money out of America to being an advocate for money here in America, rebuilding our capital base? Is there tension there, or am I creating paradoxes out of thin air to build a theme?

SS: I think you’re creating a bit of a paradox out of thin air. First of all, there’s a policy question — if you have a working class trying to get money to support their family, how can they do that as efficiently as possible?

The bigger issue is the profound lie of globalization. The calculus that globalization got wrong is this idea that we can do the innovation and “they” can do the production — “they” make the things, we do the innovation. The problem is that innovation is a consequence of productivity, if you stop making the thing, you cede the stimulus required to do the innovation around the thing.

The example I always give young computer scientists is, what do you think motivated Google to do the research behind “ Attention Is All You Need “? If you talk to that team, they wanted the 3% improvement in Google Translate. You cannot think of something more prosaic leading to something more profound. So we should be very careful where we give up — we buy a little too much into comparative advantage and give up the stimulus for production.

Why do you think — what leads to that mistake of thinking that it’s okay to just own the inputs and not worry about the outputs?

SS: Because at the margin, it’s true. At the margin, you can hire WuXi as a cheap set of hands at the lab bench to do a little bit of work. But at the limit, that’s a transfer of knowledge. At every increment it seems to make sense — you’re still doing the innovation — until one day you wake up and realize, “Oh, I don’t have it anymore”.

Diffusing Intelligence

You’re the only Stratechery interview that I’ve offered a job to. You sent over a list of questions you wanted me to talk about, and I have to say they’re really good — I did ask if you wanted to prepare all my interviews going forward, I don’t think I got a response, maybe the email got lost.

SS: (laughing) I’m thinking about it.

Okay, good. Well, let’s drill in — we’ll take your outline, why not, go through it and talk about it, and I think there are themes that might emerge. So number one, and this is from Shyam Sankar, does this count as a Shyam bomb, by the way, the long extended email detailing what we should talk about?

SS: It’s not nearly vitriolic enough, so you’re spared.

Got it, that makes sense. Number one, is the AI industry solving the wrong bottleneck? You argue we are over-investing intellectually in the supply of intelligence and under-investing in diffusion. Tell me what you mean.

SS: If you thought about a crass metaphor of AI through electricity — there are people who generate the electrons, the power producers — for electricity to have any impact on our economy, there needed to be other people who built machine tools that run on those electrons. And that led to a profound revolution. Not only would you introduce one piece of machinery into your factory, you’d start redesigning your factories around the fact that we have electrons.

Baked into that is the idea that eventually this stuff will diffuse, eventually there will be economic value.

blogs.title: Meta Earnings, Muse and the Frontier, Musebook
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Meta's earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta's spending on compute.
blogs.content:
Meta's earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta's spending on compute.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

I joined Myke Hurley on the Cortex Podcast to discuss how I write Stratechery. Then, I joined John Collison on Cheeky Pint to ( again ) interview United CEO Scott Kirby . Both podcasts were recorded a couple of weeks ago but just posted in the last few days.

On to the Update:

Meta Earnings

From Bloomberg :

Meta Platforms Inc. shares fell after Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg told investors the company would bet even more aggressively on artificial intelligence. During its quarterly earnings report Wednesday, the social-media giant boosted its capital spending plans for the year and announced a new class of nonvoting stock that could ultimately be used to help pay for acquisitions and other expenses. The moves show that Meta has confidence that its already-stratospheric spending on AI is bearing fruit. After struggling to persuade investors to accept ballooning costs, Meta has made headway with its technology in recent months, especially with a new AI agent called Muse. Zuckerberg pointed to that progress as reason to keep plowing ahead.

Meta is indeed plowing ahead; from the Wall Street Journal earlier this week:

Meta Platforms unveiled a plan to raise up to $95 billion in waves of stock offerings, as the company embarks on a cash-raising spree to fund its massive investments in artificial-intelligence infrastructure. The Facebook parent said Monday it will launch roughly $35 billion in public offerings, comprising $22.5 billion of Class A common stock and $12.5 billion of depositary shares representing mandatory convertible preferred stock.

Meta also plans to establish an at-the-market stock offering program of up to $60 billion, potentially beginning in the first quarter of 2027. That is the program by which the company will create a new class of nonvoting stock, a move it previously announced. The company expects to sell shares of its new “Class C” stock over time, though Meta said Monday it hasn’t finalized the arrangement.

One year ago, after Meta’s 3Q 2025 earnings, I wrote that the company was realizing the true cost of Reality Labs :

What I also think is happening is that Meta is finally paying the price for the billions of dollars it has spent on Reality Labs with precious little financial return to show for it. Yes, investors have long grumbled at how much money Meta has spent on AR and VR, but ultimately I think Zuckerberg has gotten a pass; even the stock market freakout in 2022 was more about TikTok and ATT than about the Metaverse (the Metaverse spending was taken as an indication that Meta’s core business was faltering).

This time, however, Zuckerberg once again seems to be asking for a blank check, and given that the last blank check is growing, not cashing, I think that investors are hesitant about writing another one. Again, I’m not sure this is necessarily fair — Meta is clearly leveraging more compute effectively in its ad business, and AI is not the Metaverse — but unless Zuckerberg wants to become the world’s biggest ad business salesman he’s going to need to show some tangible evidence sooner or later that Meta can in fact win on product.

What a difference a year makes. Meta has indeed shown up asking for that blank check, and just for context, this now-$97.5 billion worth of equity offerings very nearly matches all of Reality Labs’ recorded losses. Now, to be fair, those recorded losses only go back to Q4 2019; Meta bought Oculus for $2 billion in 2014, which is to say the cumulative losses since then are higher than the $100.8 billion on the books. Still, the fact we are in the same ballpark points to how much larger the AI expenditures are in aggregate.

What is different is that I strongly believe that Meta has earned the benefit of the doubt, and not just because I have been on the record since 2024 that Meta had arguably the largest AI opportunity ; rather, go back to what Zuckerberg wrote in July 2025 when Meta’s AI efforts seemed dead in the water, even as the company was spending millions of dollars on talent and making billions of dollars worth of compute commitments:

As profound as the abundance produced by AI may one day be, an even more meaningful impact on our lives will likely come from everyone having a personal superintelligence that helps you achieve your goals, create what you want to see in the world, experience any adventure, be a better friend to those you care about, and grow to become the person you aspire to be. Meta’s vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone. We believe in putting this power in people’s hands to direct it towards what they value in their own lives.

This is distinct from others in the industry who believe superintelligence should be directed centrally towards automating all valuable work, and then humanity will live on a dole of its output. At Meta, we believe that people pursuing their individual aspirations is how we have always made progress expanding prosperity, science, health, and culture. This will be increasingly important in the future as well. The intersection of technology and how people live is Meta’s focus, and this will only become more important in the future. If trends continue, then you’d expect people to spend less time in productivity software, and more time creating and connecting. Personal superintelligence that knows us deeply, understands our goals, and can help us achieve them will be by far the most useful.

It is difficult to overstate how important Muse is, not just in terms of what it represents in terms of AI , or the business opportunities , but specifically that it represents Zuckerberg delivering on his promise in a way that Reality Labs has never come close to doing. Yes, investors are grumbling about Meta’s spending plans and this equity raise, which is reasonable given that dilution is, as I noted yesterday , forcing existing shareholders to pay up. If Muse didn’t exist, however, and if it didn’t hew so closely to exactly what Zuckerberg promised he would build, I think there would be a revolt by the stock market.

---

Presented by

When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: every Substack creator is also a Stripe customer, and that’s the case for many other creator platforms.

Of course, they didn’t succeed because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

---

Muse and the Frontier

From Artificial Analysis on X :

Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, featuring 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets.

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today. v5 is our biggest upgrade since v4 launched in January. With v5, 60% of the Index is now based on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers.

Alongside Intelligence Index v5, we’re launching the Artificial Analysis Progress Index v1, which tracks model capability over time on one continuous scale.

New benchmarks are, in my estimation, the only benchmarks worth paying attention to, because by virtue of being new, models have not been bench-maxxed, i.e. trained specifically to do well on the benchmarks in question. To that end, here is the Index :

The rankings here roughly match my sense of the landscape and, for what it is worth, my experience:

Opus 5.5 is the best model, although the GPT-6 family is very strong.

Chinese models are really not that close to the frontier (although Kimi K3.1 Pro’s showing is impressive; it’s also the largest Chinese model by far). This is obvious when you use them (which is to say that using them makes you very aware of what bench-maxxing means in practice).

Google and Meta are very much on the frontier, albeit not state-of-the-art (Grok, meanwhile, is falling far behind).

Meta’s comeback here is notable, and necessary: for all of the product sensibility that goes into Muse, it really does feel like the model is just barely good enough, which makes sense when you see Muse Spark Open’s score on this chart; you also realize why the release of Muse Wonder was an important milestone, and what a difference it is going to make when Meta figures out how to serve it efficiently to more users. Zuckerberg said on the earnings call :

And then there’s just continuing to increase the value in the product which I think we will largely do by continuing to develop new models. That’s why I mentioned that we launched Muse first on Muse Spark, and that’s what is currently the default across the free tier. And we rolled out Muse Wonder, and people can access that in the paid tier today. And we know that it performs a lot better, so we’re working on getting a more efficient version of Muse Wonder that we’ll be able to roll out more broadly. But you can imagine just as we iterate forward in two, three models into the future, when you have significantly higher intelligence and capability to solve many more problems for people and the ability to deliver that at a much more affordable price point, I think that that’s going to just unlock a lot more value to people. So we’re very excited about that.

Muse presents to investors a very binary question: if you think that it is a tremendous opportunity, then you must support Meta’s compute spending, because spending is the only way to get better models. That was, as I noted yesterday , the most important takeaway from Anthropic’s S-1: R&D compute is massively larger than inference compute, and its share of the total compute bill is growing. Yes, serving Muse will cost a lot; making Muse great will, at least for a while, cost more.

This also, I must admit, gave me more sympathy for Meta’s enterprise aspirations. The project is, to be clear, entirely solipsistic ; Zuckerberg said as much in his opening remarks:

One other note on compute economics is that since training is a large fixed cost, now that we have leading models, we want to serve as much high-margin inference demand as possible. That is why we are building the Meta Enterprise Platform, led by CJ Desai. Muse Wonder and even more advanced models that we are training can serve additional high-margin services beyond the Muse network, including our API, Muse Code, and other enterprise services.

What I mean by solipsistic is that the enterprise initiative is coming into being not because enterprise customers are asking for it, but because Zuckerberg sees the need to maximize the number of call options on the massive training costs he’s incurring. What makes me more sympathetic is that it is more likely than I thought that there will be enough inference compute to go around if this effort hits (just because the share of compute going to inference is likely lower than I originally thought). If I’m honest, I still think it’s an unnecessary distraction, but sometimes solipsism is self-preservation!

That noted, the most compelling argument for investors opposed to this spending is not that Muse doesn’t need it, but that Meta actually doesn’t need Muse. CFO Susan Li started out her summary of the company’s business results thusly:

Q3 Total Family of Apps revenue was $64.2 billion, up 26%. Q3 Family of Apps ad revenue was $63.1 billion, up 26% on both a reported and constant currency basis. In Q3, the tota...

blogs.description: Anthropic's IPO is finally here; the core business is very profitable, but competition may eat all of the profits, even as investors are set up for endless dilution.
blogs.content:
Anthropic's IPO is finally here; the core business is very profitable, but competition may eat all of the profits, even as investors are set up for endless dilution.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

On last week’s episode of Sharp Tech — also available on video on YouTube and Spotify — Andrew and I discussed Netflix, security, and our experience with Meta’s VR glasses; then on Sunday’s subscriber-only mailbag we covered Ubiquiti, the Tim Cook era in retrospect, and Y2K.

On to the Update:

Anthropic S-1

From Bloomberg :

Anthropic PBC filed for its long-awaited IPO, a landmark moment in the artificial-intelligence industry that is growing ever-hungrier for cash to power ahead. The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing Monday with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

The filing moves Anthropic a step closer to being the first company focused primarily on developing the most advanced AI models to go public. Anthropic and some of its shareholders are offering stock in the IPO, according to the filing. The amount of shares they’re offering will be disclosed in a later filing.

Anthropic’s IPO will serve as a litmus test for how much investor demand exists for new equity tied to the AI trade, after optimism surrounding the technology helped power a four-year bull market in US stocks. Just two hours before Anthropic’s filing, Meta Platforms Inc. said it is seeking to raise as much as $95 billion from selling common and preferred stock in one of the largest equity offerings in history. Earlier this year, Google-parent Alphabet Inc. targeted raising as much as $85 billion in equity. Anthropic is expected to be followed onto public markets next year by its main competitor, OpenAI.

Numbers, finally — albeit somewhat incomplete ones. The figures provided are through June 30, i.e. the end of Anthropic’s major growth spurt; those numbers go stale on November 12 and will have to be updated if Anthropic doesn’t list by then — current expectations are the week of November 16.

Anthropic has in many respects timed this listing perfectly, thanks to the explosion in its top-line revenue in the first half of this year which, combined with the company’s delay in securing compute, led to extremely impressive margins (more on these in a moment); it will be interesting if somewhat slower growth in the 3rd quarter puts a damper on the listing (or possibly a revelation that Opus 5.5 re-accelerated growth turbocharges it). Revenue growth is, needless to say, a very big deal.

The Cost of Compute

The most interesting financial numbers were absolutely buried in the S-1 , all the way down on F-39 in the “Consolidated Financial Statements”; that is where Anthropic actually broke out its costs by function:

The two most interesting are Cost of Revenue and Research and Development, because that is where the company’s compute costs lie (along with Sales and Marketing, which is where the cost of free access is housed). Those still aren’t entirely clear numbers, particularly because Research and Development contains personnel costs, but you can make some assumptions to get to the following estimate (I subtracted the Cost of Revenue and estimated free inference — I used half of Sales & Marketing — from total compute to come up with R&D compute):

There are some really interesting takeaways here.

This is a real tech company , in that Anthropic has meaningful leverage on its cost to serve. In the first half of this year the company had gross margins of 85%.

Gross margins are inflated because Anthropic reports gross revenue from access to its models sold through AWS, Azure, and Google; those costs are in Sales and Marketing, and may be somewhere around 37% on around half their revenue. Still, these are real tech company margins, at least once revenue is big enough.

Anthropic’s compute costs are dominated by R&D. Moreover, the cost of R&D compute is increasing faster than the cost of inference, at least over the last year.

What this means is that Anthropic in isolation seems like an incredible business; the challenge, however — and one reason why the company might want the industry to “pace the frontier” — is that the cost of R&D compute is the variable that is arguably the most out of their control. The scale of Anthropic’s investment in R&D compute is a function of competition; those revenue figures ultimately rest on Anthropic having frontier models, at least for now, which means ever more compute.

This also gives a different spin to the idea of recursive self-improvement, i.e. the process where AI improves itself. Anthropic is already an RSI organism, at least from a financial perspective: the company is the biggest consumer of its own compute and its own AI, all in the service of building an even better AI. Folks complain about circular financing in the AI trade; the reality is that the companies at the core of that trade are the ultimate ouroboros, where their long-term financial upside is dependent on not eating themselves completely!

To that end, it is interesting to think about how the approximately $855 billion in future compute costs Anthropic has committed to might be allocated; the assumption is that the vast majority of that money is for inference, but if current trends hold it is R&D compute that will consume a major part of it.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: every Substack creator is also a Stripe customer, and that’s the case for many other creator platforms.

Of course, they didn’t succeed because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

---

Who Is Paying?

That noted, the $855 billion number is an estimate — basically I added up all disclosed commitment categories, which could have some overlap — and not locked in stone:

$269.4 billion is non-cancelable minimum cloud spend with AWS, Google, and Microsoft.

$161.2 billion is non-cancelable equipment leases with Broadcom that must be paid when equipment is ready.

$21.0 billion in short-term commitments to unspecified counterparties is non-cancelable.

$85.9 billion is committed to Nscale and Lambda as capacity is accepted.

Up to $120.5 billion in commitment to SpaceXAI is cancelable with 90 days notice starting in 2027.

The remaining ~$200 billion is a catch-all for unknown commitments.

The hyperscaler angle is particularly interesting. First, those are the contracts that are the most concrete. Second, those contracts were, in the case of Amazon and Google (and Broadcom), signed in conjunction with Note Purchase Agreements (NPAs), in which the hyperscalers basically loan money to Anthropic with the right to convert that debt into equity. That money, of course, flows right back to the hyperscalers to rent compute.

So who is actually paying? Despite those incredible margins, Anthropic reported an $80 billion loss in the first half of this year, because its liability to Amazon under earlier NPAs was marked to the dramatically increasing market price of the stock Amazon was entitled to, resulting in a $72 billion fair value charge. That right there is the clue: Anthropic isn’t out extra cash because its valuation increased; rather investors were diluted.

Anthropic has $77 billion in NPAs which have not yet been drawn on, which is to say that $80 billion “loss” is only the beginning, at least if the valuation continues to increase. That money is, whenever it is borrowed for compute from the lender, ultimately paid for by investors being diluted (although there will likely never be as large of a “loss”, which is to say a corresponding gain, for those other NPAs — that was an all-time investment by Amazon); meanwhile, every time Anthropic’s valuation increases by 50%, 2% of shares may go to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund; all of this is before we get to the actual capital that Anthropic hopes to raise in this initial public offering, and the future equity offerings that will likely follow.

In short, what is happening with this IPO, along with Meta’s equity offering, which followed on Google’s offering earlier this year , is that public market investors are being asked to pay for the AI buildout that the credit market is increasingly nervous about, and those payments are not necessarily straightforward. The price isn’t just shares, but the fact those shares will inevitably represent a continually decreasing share of the company.

This is why the revenue numbers will matter. In the long run, revenue does, of course, need to cover costs; in the short run, however, revenue will matter for the narrative which public stockholders will need to buy, such that they buy assets that are set up from the beginning for dilution. That will be fine if the valuation increase outpaces the dilution, and, to be fair, it is entirely reasonable to decide stock in a frontier lab is, no matter the price, a reasonable call option on seemingly unlimited upside. That’s the thing about revenue growth: when it’s up-and-to-the-right you can get away with anything.
